title: The Theories That Nobody Kills
author: Becky Allen
summary: Becky Allen, drawing on philosopher Paul Meehl's 1978 critique of soft psychology, argues that education research has a structural problem: large datasets like the National Pupil Database make it trivially easy to detect statistically significant but theoretically meaningless associations, because education theories tend to make vague predictions ("this will help learning") rather than the risky, specific predictions that could actually be proven wrong. She shows that even randomized controlled trials, the field's methodological gold standard, only answer whether an intervention worked, not why, leaving rival theoretical explanations for the same result permanently unresolved. This is why faded educational theories, learning styles, discovery learning, whole language, never die but simply cycle back into fashion after a decade, since they were never decisively falsified in the first place, and why the common defense that "theories complement each other" is, in Allen's view, a way of dressing up unresolved intellectual disagreement as maturity. She proposes a fix modeled on cognitive load theorist John Sweller's own move to narrow his theory's scope (abandoning "germane cognitive load" once it could explain any result), arguing education needs theories specific enough to be proven wrong, and studies designed to place rival theories at genuine risk against each other.
points: Allen's central diagnostic borrows Meehl's rain analogy directly: weak theories (it will rain sometime in April) are almost impossible to falsify, while strong theories (it will rain exactly this much on this day) risk being definitively wrong, and most education theories are built like the former.

She identifies why faded educational theories keep returning rather than staying dead: because they were never decisively refuted, only abandoned from boredom, 'there is nothing to stop the revival gaining momentum' a decade later under altered language.

Her sharpest institutional critique targets the field's favorite escape hatch, calling different theories 'complementary' rather than rival, arguing this framing 'turns our failure to resolve competing explanations into some kind of intellectual maturity' rather than acknowledging unfinished work.

The Sweller case study (abandoning 'germane cognitive load' once it could explain any positive instructional result) is offered as the rare model of a theorist deliberately narrowing his own theory's scope to make it falsifiable again, which Allen holds up as the exception to the field's usual pattern of theoretical bloat.
quotes: A weak theory predicts it will rain sometime in April. A strong theory or risky prediction specifies which days it will rain and how much rain will fall. Weak theories have so many ways to be right, after all, there are so many opportunities for it to rain in April.
But the RCTs that we chose to run only answered the technological questions: did the programmes work? They didn't answer the theoretical questions: why did the programmes work?

Learning styles, discovery learning, whole language, multiple intelligences, growth mindset style ideas can disappear from respectable discussion for a decade, but then reappear years later in altered language. They were never decisively rejected, and so there is nothing to stop the revival gaining momentum.

Calling all three situations complementarity prevents us from discovering which one we face. It means everyone gets to create and keep their favourite theory. And it turns unfinished intellectual work into mature-sounding conclusions.

So, Sweller narrows the scope of cognitive load theory to strengthen its theoretical power. It's a rare moment of a theorist killing a piece of his own theory to strengthen it, against the usual pattern of endless theoretical bloat.
A theory that can expand to accommodate every content, interaction and outcome has not explained the complexity. It has merely redescribed it.
